_about: THE CONNECTION CONTRACT, in the form the gate can read.
Read by tests/validate.sh's `database contract` check. One file, because
the alternative is six snippets that each restate what the settings are and
a seventh place — a README paragraph — that says what they mean, and the
three disagree the moment a fourth language is added. This file is the one
that is checked; README.md is the one that is read.
WHAT THIS FILE IS FOR
Every generated per-language config must CARRY the required settings and
must NOT carry the pooler workarounds. Both directions are asserted, per
language, against the file named below. The second half is the half that
matters most: a service carrying `prepare: :unnamed` looks correct and is
wrong, because kit runs no pooler and that flag trades real performance
for compatibility with a component that is not in the path.
A comment saying 'remember to set prepare: :unnamed' is not a contract.
A comment saying 'do NOT set prepare: :unnamed, and here is why' plus a
check that fails the build when it appears IS one.
WHAT IS NOT IN HERE, AND WHY
The VALUES. Timeouts and pool sizes are decisions a service makes in its
own repository, and kit's own rule is that pins are placeholders. What is
fixed here is the SETTING NAMES and the requirement to carry them — the
names are what a service and kit must agree on, and the numbers are what
the service tunes.
The pooler choice itself, beyond its name. The argument is in README.md
and the measurements are in DECISIONS.md, because an argument in a JSON
file is an argument nobody reads and a check that only checks a string.
THE ACCOUNT BOUNDARY, IN THE FORM THE GATE CAN READ.
A third block in the one contract file rather than a second contract file,
and that is this file's own argument applied: `requiredSettings` says what
every generated per-language config must CARRY, and this says what the
row-level-security substrate must CONTAIN. Two subjects, one file, one check.
Every string below is checked against the file with SQL COMMENTS STRIPPED.
That is the rule this repository already states about `-count=1` — a check a
comment can satisfy is not a check — and it bites harder here than anywhere
else in the tree, because substrate.sql's comments quote nearly every one of
these strings while explaining why each exists. A check that read the file as
text would report the whole contract satisfied on a substrate with none of it.

required.why: THE ONE THAT IS IN NOBODY'S GUIDE. Postgres exempts a table's OWNER from its own policies, and every service in this fleet runs its migrations as its own role. Without FORCE the owner reads every account's rows while the policies read as if they were in place, and no lint in the fleet checks for it. Measured on this kit, a protected three-row table read as the owner with another tenant's identity: 1 row with FORCE, 3 without. tests/tenancy_test.sh deletes this statement and requires the OWNER half of the assertion set to go red while the LOGIN half stays green.

FORCE without ENABLE is a no-op and ENABLE without FORCE is the trap. Both, in this order, each asserted rather than assumed — and the two are asserted by the same statement list, so a substrate that enabled without forcing is caught by the token above rather than by a rule about which came first.

The `(select ...)` wrapping: one call per statement against one per candidate row. Measured on this kit, five rows and one query, 1 call wrapped and 5 bare. It is a required STRING rather than a rule because the correct spelling is one literal in one function, and a rule about parsing rendered policy qualifiers would be a second parser for a value this repository already owns.
One entry point. A substrate that also offered a weaker way to protect a table is a substrate the weaker way gets chosen from, and nothing about the weaker one would look weaker.

The seam, and the half that is transaction-local. One function a service calls once per request means one place in a codebase writes the identity GUC, and `is_local = true` is what makes a pooled connection safe: a session-level tenant variable survives the pool and hands one tenant's rows to another.

The read side of the seam, and the half whose NULL is load-bearing. No identity and an identity that owns nothing must be indistinguishable, or the boundary is an enumeration oracle — core's D33 arriving from the other end.

A policy is a filter on every candidate row, so an account-scoped table read through its primary key is still a sequential scan without an index on the column the policy filters on. Creating it inside protect_table is what stops that being a separate thing to remember.
PUBLIC holds no table privilege by default, and one statement makes the answer to "who can read this" not be "whoever the last migration remembered".

The sweep, and the only thing that keeps a service honest as it grows: a table added next month with an account_id column and no policies is named on the next run, which is the moment before it matters.

THE CREDENTIAL ENTRY POINT, and it is ONE call that protects the table exactly as `protect_table` does and then adds a fifth `for select` policy whose qualifier is the digest the caller presented. A table whose access path is ‘find the row by an unguessable value and learn the account from it’ cannot be scoped by an account it has not computed yet: `identity` measured zero rows, and a 401, for every scoped token. The policy carries the SAME predicate the caller’s query carries, which is what makes `select *` return that one row rather than the whole table. DECISIONS.md MD24 records the BYPASSRLS-role and SECURITY-DEFINER alternatives as dead for this substrate, with the reasons.

The second transaction-local GUC, and the cost of the credential path stated rather than hidden: a pool must not hand one resolution’s digest to the next connection, exactly as `begin_account/1` must not hand one tenant’s identity to the next. It takes a text digest the caller has ALREADY computed, so Postgres never learns the secret and gains no ability to derive one.

The `(select ...)` wrapping on the fifth policy too, for the same measured reason as the four account policies: one evaluation per statement against one per candidate row. Required as a string because the correct spelling is one literal in one function, and a rule about parsing rendered qualifiers would be a second parser for a value this repository already owns.

THE AUDIT, and the reason the mechanism’s scope is auditable rather than ambient: one query answers ‘which tables in this database can be read with no account’. It reads the POLICIES rather than a list, so it cannot be satisfied by a mechanism that records nothing, and it reads them through pg_depend rather than through pg_get_expr, so the answer does not depend on the reader’s search_path — the dependence that made this audit report NO credential table at all to the one role whose "$user" schema is cafaye. It deliberately does NOT answer who resolved — the digest is transaction-local — because a claim this file cannot honour is a comment pretending to be a control.
The sweep reads pg_class itself rather than trusting that protect_table ran. A sweep that only knew about tables it had created itself would be satisfied by a sweep that creates nothing.

THE MEMBERSHIP ENTRY POINT, and the reason it sits beside the credential one rather than being folded into `protect_table`. A membership table is read two ways and the ordinary predicate can only do one of them: `protect_table` answers "which rows belong to the account I am standing in", which is true, useless, and exactly wrong for "which accounts am I in" — a query that runs before any account is being stood in. Measured against a real `account_users` under identity's 00016, that query returned an empty list while every policy read as correctly installed: a green suite and an empty product screen. The policy added here is `for select` only, so a caller can discover where it belongs without gaining the ability to change who is there, and that difference is what `membership/discovery-cannot-write` exists to hold.

THE THIRD TRANSACTION-LOCAL GUC, and the reason the substrate needed one at all. Naming the CALLER is what makes a user-scoped predicate expressible; the alternatives were a SECURITY DEFINER bypass (already dead for credentials in MD24, for the same reason) or a policy that cannot say WHICH caller is asking and therefore reads every membership in the fleet. Same `is_local = true` argument as `begin_account/1`, and it inherits its cost: outside an explicit transaction the setting expires at the end of the statement that set it, so a caller that forgets the transaction reads zero memberships rather than somebody else’s.

The `(select ...)` wrapping on the discover policy too, for the same measured reason as the four account policies and the credential policy: one evaluation per statement against one per candidate row. Required as a string because the correct spelling is one literal in one function, and a rule about parsing rendered policy qualifiers would be a second parser for a value this repository already owns.

THE SECOND AUDIT, and its being SEPARATE from `credential_tables` is the point rather than duplication. There are now two ways a policy can stop requiring an account, so one query could no longer answer "can anything here be read without an account" — and merging them would report a membership table as resolvable by anybody who guesses a digest, which is the same conflation this repository keeps refusing elsewhere. Both read the POLICIES rather than a list, and both read them through pg_depend rather than pg_get_expr, so the answer does not depend on the reader’s search_path.

forbiddenWhy: `auth.uid()` is Supabase's helper, not ours. It reads a JWT claim out of a GUC, which is ONE authentication shape out of six languages — identity issues opaque session tokens, gateway verifies JWKS bearer JWTs — and a substrate that hardcoded one would be silently wrong for the other five. The seam is `begin_account/1`, and a service fills it from whatever it already authenticates. That is also why this substrate does not parse tokens: a template that guessed would be right once.

The other four are the shapes that make a policy decorative. `to public` is an unnamed role, and an unnamed policy is evaluated for every role on the cluster including the eight other services'. `for all` collapses four commands into one qualifier that can then never be widened for one of them without widening all of them. `USING (true)` and `with check (true)` are an always-permissive policy that reads in review exactly like a real one, and they are the shape every "permissive RLS policy" lint is written to flag.

requiredWhy: `set local role` is how the two halves of the assertion set are reached — the login role and the owner — and both halves are load-bearing and neither is obvious. Without the LOCAL form the role change refuses to run at all. Inside a transaction it is undone by any `exception` block it was issued from, which is a harness that silently tests the wrong role and reports a green proof; the first version of this file made exactly that mistake, by wrapping the refusals in a SECURITY DEFINER recorder that ran them as the OWNER and so succeeded at disabling the boundary it was asserting nobody could disable.

`cafaye.begin_account` is the identity seam being USED rather than read about. Every read denial in the file is meaningless without it: with no identity set, every row is hidden and every denial assertion passes.

`cafaye.unprotected_tables()` is the sweep being exercised rather than trusted, and it carries the assertion set's only POSITIVE CONTROL: that the sweep really does report a table with an account_id column and no policies. Without it the sweep's empty result is satisfied by a sweep that reports nothing at all, which is the same shape as an isolation test that only asserts "no identity reads zero rows".

`pg_temp.cafaye_assert` is the file's own recorder. Required by name because the results are collected by a function this file defines in `pg_temp`, and a proof whose results are collected by something else is a proof whose result format is whatever that something else produces — which is precisely what the six drivers would then have to know about.

`cafaye.begin_credential` is the credential seam being USED, and it is in this list because the credential half of the assertion set is meaningless as prose without it: with no digest open, every credential read is denied and the twelve rows that prove a resolution works would pass for the same wrong reason the first four would. Every read denial in this file is a claim about what a session MAY do AFTER it opens a context, and the context is the part that is easiest to leave out.

`cafaye.begin_user` is the caller seam being USED, and it is in this list for a reason the other two do not share. Those two are guards against a harness that forgets to OPEN a context and then calls every row a denial. This one guards against the opposite and quieter failure: the membership half's first row is satisfied by a substrate with no mechanism at all — which is exactly the state identity shipped in, where every assertion was green and `GET /v1/accounts` answered `[]` to an owner. So the twelve rows that prove a discovery works have to name a caller to be about anything.
isolation.spineWhy: THE SHAPE, and it is four assertions per role rather than one. A request with no identity reading zero rows is satisfied by a table with no policy at all, which is the bug. A request with its own identity reading its own rows is satisfied by a policy that permits everything. Only together are they the property. Every one of these eight names must be CONSTRUCTED in the script as well as listed in assertions.txt — a manifest naming an assertion the script never makes is a manifest reporting completeness for a proof that does not contain it — and the owner/ four exist because the login/ four pass on a substrate with no FORCE at all.

assertions.why: The manifest all six drivers compare against, and the reason completeness is a SET rather than a COUNT. A count of 24 is compatible with 24 of the wrong 24, and a driver asserting only "no red rows" is satisfied by a proof that had been cut down to three assertions by an earlier commit nobody read. The check below reads this file and isolation.sql and fails on a difference in EITHER direction.

drivers.why: The six per-language tests. Each runs isolation.sql, reads the result table it creates, and then asserts that the assertion NAMES it got back are EXACTLY assertions.txt. They are thin on purpose — the assertions are about Postgres, not about a language — and thin is safe ONLY because of that comparison, so the check below requires every language kit templates to carry a driver, requires each driver to actually READ both files, and requires the result-table name to appear in code.
drivers.mustReadWhy: Checked on the SAME LINE as one of the language's own read forms, which is the whole difficulty. A first version asked only whether the file mentioned the name, and every driver mentions both in its own header comment — the header is WHY the driver is thin — so a driver whose read had been deleted was reported clean. A second version asked whether the file contained a read ANYWHERE, and every driver satisfies that by reading isolation.sql, so a driver that had stopped reading assertions.txt was still clean. Both were satisfied by the exact edit they exist to catch. What this check cannot show is that the driver EXECUTES the script it read rather than reading it and running its own query; that limit is recorded in the report rather than papered over.
drivers.mustCarryWhy: The result table isolation.sql creates. It is in code rather than in a comment because it is the thing a driver queries AFTER running the proof, and a driver that never asks for it is not running this proof at all. Every other list this check iterates has an empty-list guard for the same reason: a list that is empty makes the loop over it a no-op that passes, which is how a check ends up green having read nothing.

pooler.summary: One cluster, direct connections, a stated connection budget, and per-role blast-radius limits. No transaction-mode pooler.
forbiddenWhy: These are the settings a service adds to SURVIVE a pooler, and kit runs
no pooler. Each one is a real setting with a real purpose; none of them has
They are forbidden rather than merely discouraged because their cost is
simple_protocol` both disable named prepared statements, which makes every
execution re-parse and re-plan. A service carrying one of them is SLOWER
and looks fine, and the only way to notice is to look for the flag.
A check that lists them is also the cheapest possible tripwire for the
real failure: somebody reading a blog post, or a copied `docker-compose.yml`
from a company that does run PgBouncer, adding a pooler workaround to a
generated config in a fleet that has no pooler. The diff is one line and
the flag is in this file.
are in the list because they are pgbouncer.ini KEYWORDS: a service carrying
one of them has, in effect, configured a pooler it does not have.

requiredSettings.why: THE ONE THAT IS NOT OPTIONAL. Nine services share one pg_stat_activity, and without an application_name a query in it cannot be attributed to any of them. It is also what a slow-query log, a pg_stat_statements breakdown, and an operator asking whose query is this all read.
requiredSettings.servedBy: the service name, which is also its database name and its role name

requiredSettings.why: One service's runaway query occupies shared resources until it finishes. On its own machine that is its own outage; on a shared cluster it is everybody's. The cluster sets this per role as a backstop, so a service that omits it is still bounded — this is the first line, not the only one.
requiredSettings.servedBy: KIT_POSTGRES_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS in the cluster, as the backstop

requiredSettings.why: THE SHARED-CLUSTER KILLER. One forgotten BEGIN holds a snapshot open, which blocks VACUUM and grows every table on the box. With one database per machine that is one service's problem; with one cluster it is nine services' problem, and it is silent until the disk fills.
requiredSettings.servedBy: KIT_POSTGRES_IDLE_IN_TRANSACTION_TIMEOUT_MS in the cluster, as the backstop

boundedPool.why: This service's share of the cluster's connection budget, expressed as a cap inside the process. It is the INNER of two caps: the cluster's per-role `ALTER ROLE … CONNECTION LIMIT` is the outer one, and the two must agree in the direction that is safe — an inner cap larger than the outer one does not give the service more connections, it gives it errors.
boundedPool.tokensWhy: One token per language's own spelling, because the check is over GENERATED OUTPUT and each driver names this differently. A single canonical token would have meant rewriting each snippet to carry a token its driver does not use, which is decoration rather than a contract. `pool_size` carries NO leading colon because the check now strips comments before looking: the Elixir snippet's real setting is `pool_size: @pool_size,` and the `:pool_size` spelling existed only in its prose, so the token was being satisfied by a comment and reported the bounded pool as absent once the comments went.

languages.parserWhy: The one language whose connection config is DATA rather than code, so `yaml.safe_load` is its parser — and it is not an ERB template, because a file with `<%= ENV.fetch(...) %>` in it is not YAML and the parse check would fail on every run. Substitute the URL at read time.

languages.alsoForWhy: bun runs the same node-postgres driver, so it ships THIS file rather than a second one. A near-identical bun.ts would be two files to keep in step for no difference in behaviour.
